children: A federal judge in Florida has secured the dismissal of a judicial misconduct complaint that accused him of undermining confidence in the impartiality of the courts through his staunch advocacy for Israel and comments describing the keffiyeh, long a symbol of Palestinian nationalism, as a “terrorism scarf."
Chief U.S. Circuit Judge William Pryor of the Atlanta-based 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Tuesday

against Miami-based U.S. District Judge Roy Altman, saying judges are allowed under the judicial code of conduct to engage in non-law related activities and that a prohibition on engaging in political ones only applied to ones related to elections.

"Subject to limited exceptions provided by the Code, federal judges — like others — enjoy federal civil rights, including the freedoms of speech and of the press and the free exercise of religion as guaranteed by the First Amendment to the Constitution of the United States," Pryor wrote.

Altman, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, has frequently appeared on TV and podcasts and has been an active social media poster following the release in April of his book "Israel on Trial: Examining the History, the Evidence, and the Law."

That book and his numerous media appearances formed the basis of a judicial misconduct complaint that was filed last month by Florida lawyer Katherine Giannamore alleging he had engaged in a sustained pattern of conduct "that has undermined public confidence in the integrity, impartiality, and independence of the federal judiciary."

She alleged that he had used judicial resources to promote his book, used his social media accounts to platform groups who are motivated by anti-Muslim and anti-Arab bias, and promoted a speech hosted by a group that describes itself as dedicated to combating "the infrastructure of lawful Islamism.”

The complaint pointed to other instances of conduct she alleged reflected anti-Muslim bias or threatened the judiciary's integrity, including by referring to the keffiyeh as a "terrorism scarf" and by inviting other federal judges for "education mission" trips to Israel.

At Altman's request, Pryor with Tuesday's order made public a response the judge had made to Giannamore's complaint, which he said was "baseless" and "leaked to the press in a transparent attempt to damage my reputation," pointing to a post on the blog Above the Law about the complaint, which would normally not be public.

He said claims that he used judicial resources for his book were false, as its acknowledgments section made clear that a team of former law clerks and interns, not current ones, helped him with research

He said there was no ethical requirement that the trips he and other judges took to Israel had to "offer the viewpoints of both America’s closest regional ally (Israel) and the terrorist proxy (Hamas) of America’s most powerful regional adversary (Iran)."

As for the scarf comment, Altman did not deny making it but said he had been "referring to students on college campuses — many of them neither Arab nor Muslim — who don the keffiyeh during campus protests, often while advocating for the genocide of Jews by shouting hateful phrases."

Giannamore in a statement said she was "frankly not surprised that Judge Pryor issued a swift dismissal because as we have seen over several months, the judiciary and legal community do not take this form of racism seriously."

"Judge Altman's statements like 'terrorist scarf' and nearly daily use of his office to broadcast himself live from judicial chambers on far-right media was all out in the open, promoted widely by him," she said.
